transcript.text: We’ll be arriving at Branley Castle in about five minutes, but before we get there I’ll give you a little information about the castle and what our visit will include.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: So in fact there’s been a castle on this site for over eleven hundred years.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The first building was a fort constructed in 914 AD for defence against Danish invaders by King Alfred the Great’s daughter, who ruled England at the time.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: In the following century, after the Normans conquered England, the land was given to a nobleman called Richard de Vere, and he built a castle there that stayed in the de Vere family for over four hundred years.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: However, when Queen Elizabeth I announced that she was going to visit the castle in 1576 it was beginning to look a bit run down, and it was decided that rather than repair the guest rooms, they’d make a new house for her out of wood next to the main hall.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: She stayed there for four nights and apparently it was very luxurious, but unfortunately it was destroyed a few years later by fire.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: In the seventeenth century the castle belonged to the wealthy Fenys family, who enlarged it and made it more comfortable.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: However, by 1982 the Fenys family could no longer afford to maintain the castle, even though they received government support, and they put it on the market.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It was eventually taken over by a company who owned a number of amusement parks, but when we get there I think you’ll see that they’ve managed to retain the original atmosphere of the castle.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: When you go inside, you’ll find that in the state rooms there are life-like moving wax models dressed in costumes of different periods in the past, which even carry on conversations together.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: As well as that, in every room there are booklets giving information about what the room was used for and the history of the objects and furniture it contains.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The castle park’s quite extensive.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: At one time sheep were kept there, and in the nineteenth century the owners had a little zoo with animals like rabbits and even a baby elephant.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Nowadays the old zoo buildings are used for public displays of painting and sculpture.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The park also has some beautiful trees, though the oldest of all, which dated back 800 years, was sadly blown down in 1987.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Now, you’re free to wander around on your own until 4.30, but then at the end of our visit we’ll all meet together at the bottom of the Great Staircase.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’ll then go on to the long gallery, where there’s a wonderful collection of photographs showing the family who owned the castle a hundred years ago having tea and cakes in the conservatory – and we’ll then take you to the same place, where afternoon tea will be served to you.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Now if you can take a look at your plans you’ll see Branley Castle has four towers, joined together by a high wall, with the river on two sides.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Don’t miss seeing the Great Hall.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: That’s near the river in the main tower, the biggest one, which was extended and redesigned in the eighteenth century.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: If you want to get a good view of the whole castle, you can walk around the walls.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The starting point’s quite near the main entrance – walk straight down the path until you get to the south gate, and it’s just there.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Don’t go on to the north gate – there’s no way up from there.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: There’ll shortly be a show in which you can see archers displaying their skill with a bow and arrow.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The quickest way to get there is to take the first left after the main entrance and follow the path past the bridge, then you’ll see it in front of you at the end.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: If you like animals there’s also a display of hunting birds – falcons and eagles and so on.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: If you go from the main entrance in the direction of the south gate, but turn right before you get there instead of going through it, you’ll see it on your right past the first tower.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: At 3 pm there’s a short performance of traditional dancing on the outdoor stage.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: That’s right at the other side of the castle from the entrance, and over the bridge.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s about ten minutes’ walk or so.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: And finally the shop.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: It’s actually inside one of the towers, but the way in is from the outside.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Just take the first left after the main entrance, go down the path and take the first right.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: So originally, St Paul’s Island wasn’t an island, it was connected to the mainland, and mammoths and other animals like bears were able to roam around the whole area.

transcript.text: In this series of lectures about the history of weather forecasting, I’ll start by examining its early history – that’ll be the subject of today’s talk.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Ok, so we’ll start by going back thousands of years.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Most ancient cultures had weather gods, and weather catastrophes, such as floods, played an important role in many creation myths.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Generally, weather was attributed to the whims of the gods, as the wide range of weather gods in various cultures shows.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For instance, there’s the Egyptian sun god Ra, and Thor, the Norse god of thunder and lightning.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Many ancient civilisations developed rites such as dances in order to make the weather gods look kindly on them.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But the weather was of daily importance: observing the skies and drawing the correct conclusions from these observations was really important, in fact their survival depended on it.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It isn’t known when people first started to observe the skies, but at around 650 BC, the Babylonians produced the first short-range weather forecasts, based on their observations of clouds and other phenomena.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The Chinese also recognised weather patterns, and by 300 BC, astronomers had developed a calendar which divided the year into 24 festivals, each associated with a different weather phenomenon.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The ancient Greeks were the first to develop a more scientific approach to explaining the weather.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The work of the philosopher and scientist Aristotle, in the fourth century BC, is especially noteworthy, as his ideas held sway for nearly 2,000 years.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In 340 BC, he wrote a book in which he attempted to account for the formation of rain, clouds, wind and storms.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: He also described celestial phenomena such as haloes – that is, bright circles of light around the sun, the moon and bright stars – and comets.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Many of his observations were surprisingly accurate.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For example, he believed that heat could cause water to evaporate.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But he also jumped to quite a few wrong conclusions, such as that winds are breathed out by the Earth.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Errors like this were rectified from the Renaissance onwards.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For nearly 2,000 years, Aristotle’s work was accepted as the chief authority on weather theory.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Alongside this, though, in the Middle Ages weather observations were passed on in the form of proverbs, such as ‘Red sky at night, shepherd’s delight; red sky in the morning, shepherd’s warning’.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Many of these are based on very good observations and are accurate, as contemporary meteorologists have discovered.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For centuries, any attempt to forecast the weather could only be based on personal observation, but in the fifteenth century scientists began to see the need for instruments.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Until then, the only ones available were weather vanes – to determine the wind direction – and early versions of rain gauges.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: One of the first, invented in the fifteenth century, was a hygrometer, which measured humidity.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This was one of many inventions that contributed to the development of weather forecasting.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In 1592, the Italian scientist and inventor Galileo developed the world’s first thermometer.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: His student Torricelli later invented the barometer, which allowed people to measure atmospheric pressure.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In 1648, the French philosopher Pascal proved that pressure decreases with altitude.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This discovery was verified by English astronomer Halley in 1686, and Halley was also the first person to map trade winds.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This increasing ability to measure factors related to weather helped scientists to understand the atmosphere and its processes better, and they started collecting weather observation data systematically.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In the eighteenth century, the scientist and politician Benjamin Franklin carried out work on electricity and lightning in particular, but he was also very interested in weather and studied it throughout most of his life.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It was Franklin who discovered that storms generally travel from west to east.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In addition to new meteorological instruments, other developments contributed to our understanding of the atmosphere.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: People in different locations began to keep records, and in the mid-nineteenth century, the invention of the telegraph made it possible for these records to be collated.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This led, by the end of the nineteenth century, to the first weather services.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It was not until the early twentieth century that mathematics and physics became part of meteorology, and we’ll continue from that point next week.1
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
